column2: What will the righteous Yudhishthira, king of dharma, say, and Bhimasena and Arjuna and the two sons of Madri,
hearing that Abhimanyu's son is born and born dead, as if the Pandavas were robbed by Drona's son, Vrishni?
Abhimanyu was dear to his fathers, Krishna, without doubt; hearing this, what will they say, conquered by Drona's son's weapon?
What greater sorrow can there be after this, Janardana, than Abhimanyu's son born dead, scourge of foes?
I, bowed with my head, appease you today, Krishna; look at Pritha and Draupadi, best of men.
If, having promised, you do not do the kind word, tiger of the Vrishnis, consider me dead and your promise fruitful.
If Abhimanyu's son, hero, does not live, invincible one, when you live, what shall I do with you?
Revive this son of Abhimanyu, dead, invincible one, hero of like eyes, as a cloud raining on crops.
You, Keshava, are righteous, truthful, of true valour; you should make that word true, scourge of foes.
You could revive these three dead worlds if you wished; how much more a dear stillborn child of your sister's son?
I know your power, Krishna; therefore I tell you: grant this supreme favour to the sons of Pandu.
Whether as your kinswoman, mighty-armed one, or as one whose son is slain, or as one who has taken refuge in you, you should show compassion here.
By those words, the bull among men, the lord, refreshed that person, who was scorched with heat, as if with water.
Then he quickly entered the birth chamber of your father, tiger among men, honoured with white garlands by rule.
It was set on every side with full water-pots, with ghee, brands of tinduka wood, and mustard, mighty-armed one,
with clean weapons laid down, and fires all round, with aged women and lovely ones for attendance, Achyuta,
and with skilled physicians around, hero. The radiant one saw also all the demon-destroying things placed there by rule by skilled people.
Seeing your father's birth chamber so arranged, Hrishikesha was glad and said, "Good, good."
As the Vrishni spoke thus with glad face, Draupadi went quickly to Virata's daughter and said:
Fortunate one, your father-in-law Madhusudana is coming to you, the ancient sage, of inconceivable self, invincible, near.
She, the ascetic-like, with a heart so tormented, seeing Govinda approach, lamented piteously:

Lotus-eyed one, look at the two children here bereaved: Abhimanyu and me, equally slain, Janardana.
mahabharata:14:67.13	Vrishni, slayer of Madhu, hero, I appease you with my head: revive this child of mine burned by Drona's son's weapon.
mahabharata:14:67.14	If this word had been said by the king of dharma, or by Bhimasena, or by you, lotus-eyed one,
mahabharata:14:67.15	'This reed will fall on the creature the mother did not know,' lord, I alone would have perished and this would not have come about.
mahabharata:14:67.16	What fruit does Drona's son, ill-minded, gain by cruelly felling with the Brahma weapon this child in the womb?
mahabharata:14:67.17	So I beg you, slayer of enemies, appeasing you with my head: I shall give up my life, Govinda, if this child is not revived.
mahabharata:14:67.18	Many were my hopes in him, good one, and they were slain by Drona's son; why then should I live, Keshava?
mahabharata:14:67.19	My thought was, Krishna, 'My lap will be full; I shall salute you, by good fortune.' That has been made vain.
mahabharata:14:67.20	With the heir of the fickle-eyed one dead, best of men, all my hopes in my heart, Krishna, have been made fruitless.
mahabharata:14:67.21	The fickle-eyed one was surely very dear to you, Madhusudana; see this son of his, felled by the Brahma weapon.
mahabharata:14:67.22	Ungrateful and cruel is this one, like his father, who abandoning the Pandava fortune has gone today to Yama's abode.
mahabharata:14:67.23	And I promised this at the head of battle, Keshava: 'When Abhimanyu is slain, hero, I shall come to you soon.'
mahabharata:14:67.24	I did not do it, Krishna; cruel are those who love life. Now what will Phalguni's son say to me when I come there?
Seeing her fallen, her kin and retinue slain, Kunti, afflicted with grief, and all the Bharata women cried out.
For a moment, O king, the Pandavas' dwelling became unbearable to look at, resounding with cries of distress.
For a moment, O king of kings, Virata's daughter, oppressed by grief for her son, was struck by faintness, hero.
Recovering consciousness, Uttara, bull of the Bharatas, placed that son in her lap and said:

Though the son of one who knows dharma, you know unrighteousness, since you make no salutation to the Vrishni hero.
mahabharata:14:68.7	Son, go and say my words to your father: for living beings, hero, death is hard in any way when the time has come.
mahabharata:14:68.8	I, bereft today of you, my husband and my son, live though I should die, my welfare lost, owning nothing.
mahabharata:14:68.9	Or, with the king of dharma's leave, mighty-armed one, I shall eat sharp poison or enter fire.

I do not speak falsely, Uttara; this will be true. I shall revive this child as all embodied beings watch.
mahabharata:14:68.19	I have never spoken falsely before, even in jest, nor turned back in battle; by that, let this child live.
mahabharata:14:68.20	As dharma and especially brahmins are dear to me, so let Abhimanyu's son, born dead, live.
mahabharata:14:68.21	As I do not know any opposition to Vijaya ever, by that truth let this dead child live.
mahabharata:14:68.22	As truth and dharma are always established in me, so let this dead child, Abhimanyu's son, live.
mahabharata:14:68.23	As Kamsa and Keshi were slain by me by dharma, by that truth let this boy live again here.
Thus addressed by Vasudeva, that child, bull of the Bharatas, slowly, O great king, began to move, conscious.
Then all the demons vanished, leaving that house; and a voice in the sky said, "Well done, Keshava, well done."
That weapon, blazing, went to the Grandsire; then, king of men, your father regained his life, and that child moved with such energy and strength as he had.
Then, O king, those Bharata women were glad, and by Govinda's command they had brahmins pronounce blessings.
Then all those delighted women praised Janardana, like those who have reached the far shore having got a boat.
Kunti, Drupada's daughter, Subhadra, Uttara and the other women of the lions among men were glad of mind.
There wrestlers, actors, jhallas, granthikas, couch-reciters, and groups of bards and minstrels praised Janardana with blessings that named the Kuru line, bull of the Bharatas.
Rising at the proper time, Uttara, pleased, saluted the delight of the Yadus with her son, O Bharata; and he, pleased, gave her many jewels especially.
And the other tigers of the Vrishnis, and the lord, true to his word, Janardana, gave your father a name, great king.
Banners fluttering as the wind blew seemed to show the Kurus to south and north.
And a man who had gone to the royal door proclaimed that day, "Revelry all night today, marked by jewels and ornaments."
Meeting by rule, the Pandavas with the Vrishnis together entered the city of Varanasahvaya, O king.
Heaven and earth and sky were covered by the sound of the hooves and wheels of that great army.
Putting the treasury in front, the Pandavas, glad in mind, with ministers and friends, then entered their own city.
Meeting King Dhritarashtra by rule, announcing their names, they saluted his feet.
After Dhritarashtra, the best of the Bharatas then saluted Gandhari, Subala's daughter, and Kunti, tiger among kings.
Having honoured Vidura and met the son of the vaishya woman, those heroes shone as they were honoured, lord of the people.
Then those heroes heard that most wondrous, varied, great marvel: your father's birth, Bharata.
Hearing that deed of the wise Vasudeva, they honoured Krishna, son of Devaki, worthy of honour.
There, recounting varied tales, Yudhishthira, Dharma's son, said to Vyasa:

By your grace, blessed one, I wish to use this wealth that has been brought for the great horse sacrifice.
mahabharata:14:70.14	I wish to get your leave for it, best of sages; we all depend on you and on the great soul Krishna.
[Vyasa] "I give you leave, king; do what comes next. Sacrifice with the horse sacrifice by rule, with fees given.
The Ashvamedha, king of kings, purifies from all sins; by sacrificing with it you will be free of sin, without doubt."
[Vaishampayana] So addressed, the righteous king of the Kurus Yudhishthira set his mind on undertaking the horse sacrifice, Kaurava.
Having taken leave of Krishna Dvaipayana, the king, eloquent, invited Vasudeva and said:

Devaki has a good son in you, best of men; whatever I say to you, mighty-armed Achyuta, do it here.
mahabharata:14:70.20	I enjoy the pleasures won by your power, delight of the Yadus; by valour and wisdom this earth was conquered by you.
mahabharata:14:70.21	Consecrate yourself; you are our highest teacher. When you have sacrificed, knower of dharma, I shall be free of sin, lord; you are the imperishable sacrifice, all, dharma, Prajapati.
[Vasudeva] "You alone, mighty-armed, are fit to say this, scourge of foes; my mind is settled that you are the refuge of all beings.
You shine today by dharma among the Kuru heroes; we are your subordinates, king, and you are held our teacher.
Sacrifice with my leave; the sacrifice has come to me. Employ me, Bharata, in whatever task you wish; I promise you truth, blameless one: I shall do all for you.
Bhimasena and Arjuna and Madri's two sons will have sacrificed when you have sacrificed, Bharata."
[Yudhishthira] "You know the time for the horse sacrifice truly; consecrate me then, for my sacrifice depends on you."
[Vyasa] "I, Paila, and Yajnavalkya will do the rule at its time, without doubt.
Your consecration will be on the full moon of Chaitra; let the materials be gathered for your sacrifice, best of men.
Let those versed in horse lore, charioteers and brahmins who know it examine the sacrificial horse, for the success of your sacrifice.
Having released it by the scriptures, let it travel the sea-girt earth, increasing your fame by your name, O king."
[Vaishampayana] So addressed, saying "So be it," the Pandava, lord of the earth, did all as told by the Brahmin, O king, and all the materials were provided.
Having gathered the materials, the king, Dharma's son, of immeasurable soul, reported to Krishna Dvaipayana.
Then the greatly radiant Vyasa said to the king, Dharma's son: "We are ready in time and fitness for your consecration."
[Yudhishthira] "This horse, brahmin, is let go by me to range this earth as it wishes; let arrangements be made for it.
Who will guard the horse as it roams the earth at will, sage? You should say."
[Vaishampayana] So addressed, O king, Krishna Dvaipayana said: "Younger than Bhimasena, best of all bowmen,
Jishnu, patient and bold, will guard it; he is able to conquer the earth, he who ended the Nivatakavachas.
In him are divine weapons and a divine frame, a divine bow and quivers; he will follow it.
Skilled in dharma and wealth, expert in all sciences, best of kings, he will lead your horse by the scriptures.
The prince, mighty-armed, dark, lotus-eyed, the hero, father of Abhimanyu, will follow it.
Radiant Bhimasena, son of Kunti, of immeasurable valour, and Nakula, lord of the people, are able to protect the realm.
And Sahadeva, Kaurava, the wise and greatly renowned, will duly arrange the whole household."
All that was said rightly, the upholder of the Kuru line did; and he instructed Phalguna about the horse.
[Yudhishthira] "Come, Arjuna; let this horse be guarded by you, hero. You are fit to protect it, no other man.
And the kings who may come against you, mighty-armed one, you must act so that there is no war with them, blameless one.
This sacrifice of mine should be announced by you to all the kings, mighty-armed, with the invitation: 'Come at the time.'"
Having said this, the righteous one appointed his brother Savyasachin, Bhima and Nakula as guards of the city.
And he appointed Sahadeva, lord of warriors, to the household; and Yudhishthira honoured the king Dhritarashtra.
Having performed the animal rites, consecrated, the Pandava, king of dharma, greatly radiant, shone with the priests.
The horse, for the horse sacrifice, was himself released by the Brahmin Vyasa, of immeasurable radiance, by the scriptural rule.
That king, born of Dharma, consecrated, shone then, O king, garlanded in gold, with a gold necklace, like a blazing fire.
Wearing black deer-skin, staff in hand, clad in linen, the radiant son of Dharma shone like Prajapati at the sacrifice.
So too all his priests, in like dress, O lord of the people; and Arjuna was like a blazing fire.
The white-horsed Dhananjaya, lord of the earth, by the king of dharma's command, followed that black-spotted horse by rule.
Flicking Gandiva, with iguana-skin guard on his fingers bound, lord of the earth, he followed that horse joyfully.
Down to the children, king, the city came to see the best of the Kurus about to depart, Dhananjaya.
Then a sound, great king, filling the ten directions, arose from the people looking at the son of Kunti, Dhananjaya.
There goes the son of Kunti, and the radiant horse which the mighty-armed one follows, touching his supreme bow.
The noble-minded Jishnu heard such words from those speaking: "Good fortune to you; go unharmed and come again, Bharata."
Then other men, O lord of men, said: "We do not see him in the crowd, but this bow is seen.
This is the renowned Gandiva, with terrible sound; may he go in good fortune and unharmed on a road without fear. We shall see him return," they said.
Such sweet words of men and women, uttered again and again, he heard, bull of the Bharatas.
A pupil of Yajnavalkya, skilled in sacrificial rites, a Veda-master, went with Partha for peace.
Many brahmins who were Veda-masters followed the great soul, and kshatriyas and vaishyas too.
The horse roamed the earth conquered by the Pandavas with the power of weapons, O great king, as directed, best of the good.
I shall tell you, hero, the wars that took place there for the Pandava, varied and great.
The horse, O king, with its guard, went round the earth, scourge of foes, to the north first; learn it, lord of the earth.
Trampling the lands of kings, the best of horses slowly went round, and the white-horsed great chariot-fighter with it.
There was no counting of kings then, by tens of thousands, who fought, great king, kshatriyas with kinsmen slain.
Kiratas, deformed, king, many sword-bearing archers, and other barbarians of many kinds had earlier been defeated in battle.
And noble kings, with joyful men and vehicles, many mad for war, met the son of Pandu.
So wars took place here and there, lord of the earth, between Arjuna and the kings who lived in various lands.
The great and fierce wars on both sides I shall tell of the son of Kunti, blameless one.
Knowing the sacrificial best of horses had arrived, the heroes at the border, armoured, surrounded it.
Charioteers with tied quivers, with fine adorned horses, surrounded the horse, O king, and began to seize it.
Then Kirithin, thinking of those kings' intent, scourge of foes, held back those heroes with conciliation.
Ignoring him, they all struck him with arrows; Kirithin held back those covered with darkness and passion.
Then Jishnu said, laughing as it were, "Turn back, you who do not know dharma; your life is better for you."
For that hero, about to depart, had been told by the king of dharma: "Partha, kings whose kinsmen are slain are not to be killed."
Hearing the words of the wise king of dharma, he told them, "Turn back," but they did not turn back.
Then Dhananjaya laughed, covering Suryavarman, king of the Trigartas, in the fight with a net of arrows.
The radiant young Ketuvarman, his younger brother, fought for his brother against the great-souled Pandava.
Seeing Ketuvarman rush upon him in battle, Bibhatsu, slayer of heroes, struck him with sharp arrows.
When Ketuvarman was struck, the great chariot-fighter Dhritavarman quickly came up in his chariot and showered Jishnu with arrows.
Seeing the quickness of the boy Dhritavarman, the valiant, greatly radiant Gudakesha was very pleased.
He saw him neither aiming nor drawing, but only pouring forth arrows, the son of Indra.
He honoured Dhritavarman in the battle in his mind, gladdening him for a moment in the fight.
The Kuru hero, smiling, in affection, great king, did not take the life of him who was angry like a serpent.
Thus protected by Partha of immeasurable radiance, Dhritavarman then loosed a sharp arrow at Vijaya.
Struck sorely on the hand by it, Vijaya, shooting quickly, let Gandiva drop from pain, and it fell to the ground.
As the bow fell from Savyasachin's hand, lord, it was like Indra's weapon, best of the Bharatas.
When that great divine bow fell, king, Dhritavarman laughed a loud laugh in the great battle.
Then Jishnu, filled with anger, wiped the blood from his hand, took up that divine bow and rained a shower of arrows.
Then a roaring sound touching heaven arose as beings of many kinds praised that deed greatly.
Seeing him angry like Time, the Ender and Yama, the Trigarta warriors quickly surrounded Jishnu.
Rushing in to protect Dhritavarman, they surrounded Gudakesha, and Dhananjaya grew angry there.
Then he quickly slew eighteen of their warriors with sharp iron arrows like Mahendra's thunderbolts.
Seeing them broken, Dhananjaya, laughing, hastily struck them with arrows like venomous snakes.
Their minds broken, all the Trigarta great chariot-fighters fled in all directions, struck by Dhananjaya's arrows.
They said to the tiger among men, slayer of the Samshaptakas: "We are all your servants and all in your control.
Command us, Partha, bowing, standing as messengers; we shall do all you wish, delight of the Kurus."
Understanding those words, he said to them all then: "Protect your lives, kings; accept the command."
When the horse of the Pandava's son came to the border, the king Vajradatta fought, best of the Bharatas.
The king, Bhagadatta's son, coming out of the city, stopped the horse as it came, and went toward the city.
Seeing him, the mighty-armed bull of the Kurus quickly and suddenly rushed up, flicking Gandiva.
Then the king, bewildered by arrows loosed from Gandiva, let the horse go, and then that hero ran at Partha.
Entering the city again, armoured, that best of kings mounted a chief of elephants and came out wishing to fight.
The great chariot-fighter, with a white umbrella held over his head and a white chowry waved, came forth.
Then, approaching Partha, great chariot-fighter of the Pandavas, he challenged the Kaurava in battle out of childishness and delusion.
In anger he sent the elephant, mountain-like, with rutting temples, toward the white-horsed one.
Arjuna cut those spears, before they reached him, in two and three with Gandiva-sped arrows in the sky itself.
Seeing them so cut, Bhagadatta's son quickly sent unfaltering arrows at the Pandava.
Then Arjuna, angered, sent at once gold-feathered straight arrows at Bhagadatta's son.
Pierced by them, the greatly radiant Vajradatta, sorely struck in the great battle, fell to the ground, but his memory did not leave him.
Then, mounting the chief of elephants again in battle, unflustered, desiring victory, he sent it toward Vijaya.
Then Jishnu, angered, sent at it arrows like released venomous snakes, like blazing fires.
Pierced by them, the great elephant, streaming blood, shone like the Himalaya, king of mountains, with many streams.
Then on the fourth day the mighty Vajradatta laughed a loud laugh and said these words:

Arjuna, Arjuna, stand; you will not escape me alive. Having killed you I shall duly offer water to my father.
mahabharata:14:75.4	My aged father Bhagadatta, friend of your father, was slain by you, because you disregarded his age. Today fight me, a child.
Having said this, Vajradatta, angered, O Kaurava, sent his elephant at the Pandava.
Sent forward by the wise Vajradatta, the chief of elephants rushed at the Pandava as if leaping into the sky.
With spray released from the tip of its trunk it drenched Phalguna, great king, like a dark cloud a mountain.
Sent by the king, thundering like a cloud, it rushed at Phalguna with the sound of its open mouth.
That chief of elephants, as if dancing, urged by Vajradatta, quickly reached the Kuru great chariot-fighter, king.
That best of elephants was held back by Arjuna by his valour, and stood with limbs pierced by arrows like a porcupine.
Seeing the elephant held back, the king, Bhagadatta's son, faint with rage, loosed sharp arrows at Arjuna.
But Arjuna, great king, with arrows that broke arrows held back those shot; that was as if a marvel.
Then, again greatly angry, the king, lord of Pragjyotisha, sent the chief of elephants forward as mighty as the wind.
Seeing it rush, the mighty son of Indra sent at the elephant a fiery iron arrow.
Struck sorely in its vital parts by it, the elephant, O king, suddenly fell to the ground like a mountain broken by the thunderbolt.
As it fell, that elephant, struck by Dhananjaya's arrow, shone like a great mountain entering the earth, crushed by the thunderbolt.
When Vajradatta's elephant had fallen, the Pandava said to the king on the ground, "Do not be afraid."

For Yudhishthira, the greatly radiant, told me as I set out: 'Dhananjaya, the kings are by no means to be killed.
mahabharata:14:75.22	Let it be enough for you so, tiger among men; and warriors too are not to be killed by you in battle, Dhananjaya.
mahabharata:14:75.23	The kings with all their friends are also to be told: Come and enjoy Yudhishthira's horse sacrifice.'
mahabharata:14:75.24	Hearing this word of my brother, I do not kill you, lord of the people. Rise, you have no fear; go in well-being, king.
mahabharata:14:75.25	Come, great king, when the full moon of Chaitra arrives; then will be the horse sacrifice of the wise king of dharma.
So addressed, the king, Bhagadatta's son, conquered by the Pandava, said, "So be it."
Hearing that the white-horsed one had come to their land, the kings, impatient, went to meet the bull of the Pandavas.
They seized the horse at the border, venomous as poison, and had no fear of Partha, who was near Bhimasena.
Not far away they met Bibhatsu, bow in hand, standing on foot beside the sacrificial horse.
Then those kings of great valour surrounded him, tigers among men, wishing to conquer, having been defeated in battle before.
Reciting their names, clans and varied deeds, they covered Partha with showers of arrows.
Your city should be well guarded, with strong ramparts and gates, crowded with turrets and towers, with six roads on every side.
This kingdom, Partha, and the women and jewels, and my dear life, all these I shall give up, slayer of foes.
Then he satisfied all those twice-born with fees, and honoured by the king they went as they had come.
